candidates.attacker_control: Any untrusted filename/path string supplied to FilenameUtils.normalize(String), normalize(String,boolean), normalizeNoEndSeparator(...) or concat(...) by a consuming application (e.g. an uploaded filename, path request parameter, or archive entry name). The strings '//../<name>' (POSIX) or '\\\\..\\<name>' (Windows) are fully attacker-controlled; no repository-internal caller is required because these are public library APIs.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: failIfNullBytePresent (lines 985-993) only rejects NUL bytes, not '..'. getPrefixLength rejects '///' (posUnix==2) and invalid drive letters, but accepts '.'/'..' as a hostname. doNormalize does correctly remove or null out '..' for non-UNC inputs, so the flaw is specific to the '//' prefix path. The javadoc's own example '//server/../bar --> null' is still satisfied only because there the '..' lies after a real hostname (prefix=9); with '..' itself as the hostname the check is evaded. A repository-wide search found no hostname validation helper. I did not execute code, so the trace is static and downstream exploitability depends on the consuming application and platform path resolution.
candidates.impact: Downstream applications that treat the returned value as normalized/safe can be induced to escape the intended directory: the surviving '..' is resolved by the filesystem/OS layer (POSIX resolves '//../foo' to '/foo'; chained with a base path it steps into parent directories). This permits unauthorized read/write/delete of files outside the restricted directory in consumers that rely on this API as a security control (limited-depth traversal, since the '..' must fall inside the unrecognized UNC host segment, but one or more levels can be traversed).
candidates.prerequisites: A consuming application uses one of these normalization methods as a sanitization/canonicalization step (e.g. to guarantee a path stays under a base directory or to reject '..'), then uses the returned string for filesystem access. The defect is only reachable for inputs beginning with '//' (or '\\\\') followed by '..' segments; for ordinary inputs (e.g. '/../foo', 'foo/../../bar') the code correctly returns null.
candidates.root_cause: doNormalize() only scans for '.'/'..' segments from index prefix+1/prefix+2 onward (lines 383, 392, 406). getPrefixLength() classifies '//' + <segment> + '/' as a UNC prefix and returns the length of that segment without any hostname validation (lines 674-682), so for input '//../foo' it returns 5 - i.e. '//../' is treated as the prefix. The '..' characters at indices 2-3 are therefore never inspected, are never removed, and never trigger the 'no parent path segment -> null' check at lines 409-411. The result is returned as-is at lines 438-441. No hostname whitelist/validation exists anywhere in the snapshot (search for isValidHostName returns zero matches).
candidates.title: FilenameUtils.normalize()/normalizeNoEndSeparator() leave '..' path segments intact when the input starts with a UNC-style '//' prefix
candidates.trace: Static trace of normalize("//../foo") on a POSIX system (SYSTEM_SEPARATOR='/'): (1) getPrefixLength: ch0='/' and ch1='/' enter the UNC branch (line 674); posUnix = indexOf('/',2) = 4, posWin = NOT_FOUND, so line 682 returns min(4,4)+1 = 5; no check rejects the hostname '..'. (2) doNormalize (line 348): prefix=5; the array is '//../foo' plus one appended separator (size=9); the adjoining-slash loop starts at i=prefix+1=6 (line 383), the dot-slash loop at 6 (line 392) and the double-dot loop at prefix+2=7 (line 406) - all after indices 2-3 where the '..' sits inside the prefix, so it is never examined; (3) size(9) > prefix(5) and lastIsDirectory=false, so line 441 returns new String(array,0,size-1) = "//../foo" - the input unchanged, still containing '..'. Control case demonstrates the intended contract: for '/../foo' the double-dot loop hits i==prefix+2 and returns null (lines 409-411), and the javadoc (lines 155-188) promises '..' removal or null.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution or downstream application was tested; exact filesystem resolution of the '//..' prefix is platform-dependent; the severity depends on how a consumer turns the normalized string into a File path. The public API entry points (normalize at 194/241, normalizeNoEndSeparator at 288/335, concat at 485, equals(...,normalized,...) at 1154) are confirmed in source, but no in-repo callers exist (this is a library).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') - path normalization bypass

coverage_summary: Scope: 164 repository files (118 Java under src/main/java, plus XML/site/docs/build files; pom.xml declares commons-io 2.6). Relation index: 163/164 files indexed, 118 Java files parsed, 0 parse errors, 1 source file missing from the index; the index provides syntax containment/call candidates only (no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, reachability, or security enforcement), and was used for navigation only. Deep review of FilenameUtils (normalize/prefix/dot-segment logic, concat, equals, helpers). Targeted review of XmlStreamReader prolog handling, ValidatingObjectInputStream/ClassLoaderObjectInputStream, FileSystemUtils exec path, and spot checks across FileUtils, IOUtils, input/output and filefilter packages. Not exhaustively reviewed: comparator package, monitor package, many input/output stream classes, and most of the 3k-line FileUtils; those were only searched/skimmed and are not claimed as reviewed in detail.
limitations: Static review only; no code execution, tests, or scanners were run, so no finding is runtime-confirmed.
The relation index has no data-flow/control-flow and 1 file is missing from it; unreported areas cannot be assumed clean.
This is a library with no in-repo callers of FilenameUtils.normalize, so exploitability depends on external consuming applications that were not available for review.
The exact OS-level resolution of paths containing a '//..' prefix is platform-specific and was reasoned about, not executed.
Only one candidate may be submitted; the rejected leads above are unconfirmed and were not exhaustively investigated.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlStreamReader potential denial of service (the area later associated with CVE-2024-47554 in this version line)
rejected_leads.reason: In this 2.6 snapshot getXmlProlog (XmlStreamReader.java lines 704-747) marks the BufferedInputStream, reads at most BUFFER_SIZE=4096 bytes in a loop bounded by 'offset < BUFFER_SIZE', and parses only xmlProlog.substring(0, firstGT+1); no unbounded read/allocation was found in source. Cannot establish the DoS from this snapshot without runtime evidence.

validateClassName runs only from resolveClass (lines 99-102); there is no resolveProxyClass/serialVersionUID/enum validation. However this class is an opt-in hardening utility whose behavior is caller-configured; no attacker-controlled accept/reject misconfiguration is present in the snapshot, so it is not a distinct source-verifiable vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: ClassLoaderObjectInputStream loads arbitrary classes during deserialization
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of the class (line 68: Class.forName with caller-supplied ClassLoader); it is not a hidden flaw, and the caller must route untrusted data to it.

Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmdAttribs) at line 573 is called with internally constructed argv arrays (e.g. df/pdx with fixed flags); the caller-supplied path is passed as a single argv element, not through a shell, so no command-injection sink is demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: '~..' style prefix swallowing (normalize("~..\\foo") keeps '..' as part of a '~user' prefix)
rejected_leads.reason: Static trace shows the '..' is consumed as part of an explicit '~user' prefix, which does not itself resolve to a parent directory; weaker and less certain impact than the '//..' case, so not selected.

summary: Snapshot is Apache Commons IO 2.6 (pom.xml version 2.6), a Java library of 164 source files (118 Java). The strongest source-verifiable issue is in FilenameUtils path normalization: a UNC-style "//" prefix allows a ".." segment to be absorbed into the "prefix" (hostname) region, so normalize()/normalizeNoEndSeparator() return a string that still contains ".." and is not nulls, contradicting the documented contract and enabling path-traversal bypass in consumers that use these APIs to sanitize untrusted paths ("//../foo" is returned unchanged). This matches the 2.6 code that was hardened in 2.7 (CVE-2021-29425). No runtime execution was performed; the finding is a static source-level lead.
